🇹🇭👀💭🚶Nearly half of the participants at an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok walked out when russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov took the floor, Reuters reports.

🚶‍♂️👋Representatives from Ukraine and several European countries staged the walkout to protest russia’s aggression and attempts to reintegrate moscow into international financial forums.

💭The protest took place on October 17 during the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank in the Thai capital.

🇷🇺🚶‍♂️As Siluanov began speaking in russian, representatives from the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and other countries left the room.

🚶Andrew Bailey, Governor of the Bank of England, also joined the protest, the British central bank confirmed.

🧐Joachim Nagel, President of the German Bundesbank, said nearly half of the delegates had left the meeting.

🤓💬“This is a very strong signal of solidarity and commitment to values. It would be best for the global economy if this unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine were to end,” Nagel said.

☝️He added that he was proud of the number of participants who joined the protest.

🚶‍♂️Andriy Pyshnyy, Governor of the National Bank of Ukraine, was among those who walked out.

🎙️💬In an interview with Reuters, Pyshnyy said he makes a point of leaving the room whenever russian officials speak at international events. He did the same in Bangkok but was surprised by the number of representatives from central banks and financial institutions who joined him.

😐💬“I was struck by the number of participants,” Pyshnyy said.

🤝He described the walkout as an important gesture of support for Ukraine.

💬“For me, it was a truly profound and emotional moment,” the NBU governor said.

☝️Pyshnyy emphasized that the protest sent an important signal to russia and its allies.

❗️“This unprovoked aggression must be stopped,” he said.

😒Not all European financial officials joined the walkout. According to two attendees, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde remained in the room.

🤓💬One European diplomat told Reuters that russia’s war against Ukraine has existential significance for Europe.

💬“The war in Ukraine is an existential issue for us in Europe. We cannot normalize relations with russia,” the diplomat said.

🇩🇪⚠️Germany had previously warned against attempts to bring russia back onto the international stage. Nevertheless, Siluanov attended meetings of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors this year. Just over a month before the Bangkok meeting, he also attended an event in the United States, marking his first in-person participation in a G20 meeting since russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

🇺🇸💩 The United States, which currently holds the G20 presidency, supports russian representatives’ participation in such events. US Deputy Secretary of the Treasury Erin Brown told Reuters that the administration considers dialogue necessary to resolve conflicts.

💬“We believe it is very important to maintain an open dialogue if you want to resolve a crisis. You cannot have a dialogue or reach a conflict resolution if no one is talking to anyone,” she said.

😳Mohammed Al-Jadaan, Saudi Arabia’s finance minister and chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee, acknowledged that a significant number of delegates had walked out during Siluanov’s remarks.

☝️However, he stressed that participants had still managed to agree on the chair’s concluding statement.

💬“We came here with a specific objective, and we achieved it. Look at the Chair’s statement: it clearly indicates that all members agreed to the document. That is what matters,” Al-Jadaan said.

According to the investigation, authorities in Sverdlovsk Oblast alone recorded 987 administrative violations and issued 218 deportation orders over a ten-day period, despite official statistics showing a 38.8% decline in crimes attributed to foreign nationals during the first eight months of the year.

### Somalia: Nearly 874,000 People Expected to Be Displaced by Flooding in the Coming Months

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that nearly 874,000 people in Somalia could be displaced between October and December 2026 due to heavy rainfall and flooding associated with the El Niño weather phenomenon, in a country already facing successive humanitarian crises.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, October 21, the organization said flooding could account for approximately 92% of the projected displacement, with the cities of Beledweyne and Galkayo facing particular risks.

The IOM also revealed that it had received only about 14% of the $16.62 million required to prepare for the floods and assist vulnerable communities.

It warned that rising floodwaters could destroy crops, contaminate drinking water sources and disrupt essential services.

🌐 New Coalition Targets Real Ownership Rights in Tokenized Stocks

Bullish, Equiniti, Alpaca, Apex Fintech Solutions and DriveWealth have formed the Issuer Sponsored Token Coalition to address a core flaw in tokenized equities: most onchain stock representations are not connected to official shareholder registers.

The coalition aims to link tokenized shares directly to companies' issuer records, preserving voting rights, dividend entitlements and corporate-action participation — rights that are currently absent in many existing tokenized stock products.

As Wall Street accelerates its push to move public equities onto blockchains, the group's work could set a standard for what "real" tokenized ownership actually means.

⚖️ SEC, CFTC and Fed Move to Write Crypto Rules After Clarity Act Fails

The Clarity Act failed to pass the Senate, prompting the SEC, CFTC, and the Federal Reserve to begin drafting crypto regulations independently within days of the vote.

With congressional legislation stalled, U.S. financial regulators are now moving to define the rules for digital assets through their own rulemaking authority rather than waiting for a legislative framework.

The shift marks a significant change in how crypto regulation may take shape in the U.S. — through agency action rather than statute, a path that carries different legal weight and is more vulnerable to future reversal.
